name: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation)
description: A dataset and evaluation method for assessing object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). POPE converts hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No questions about probing objects in images.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
citeAs: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355v3 [cs.CV], 2023.
rai:dataCollection: POPE is constructed from existing image datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) by extracting ground-truth objects either from human annotations or using automatic segmentation tools like SEEM. For each image, ground-truth objects and nonexistent objects are formulated into question templates to poll LVLMs.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images and annotations from MSCOCO validation set (2,000 randomly sampled images with more than 3 ground-truth objects), A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets. For MSCOCO, 80 objects from the segmentation challenge are considered.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Three negative sampling strategies are employed: (1) Random Sampling: randomly sample objects that do not exist in the image; (2) Popular Sampling: select the top-k most frequent objects in the whole dataset that do not exist in the current image; (3) Adversarial Sampling: rank all objects by their co-occurring frequencies with ground-truth objects and select the top-k frequent ones that do not exist in the image. The ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects is set as 1:1 for label balance.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For MSCOCO, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects in annotations were randomly selected and 6 questions were constructed for each image (l=6). Objects are extracted either from human annotations or using SEEM automatic segmentation tool. Questions are formulated using the template: 'Is there a/an <object> in the image?'
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Ground-truth objects are obtained either from existing human annotations in MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets, or through automatic segmentation using SEEM. Binary labels (Yes/No) are assigned based on whether the probed object exists in the image according to annotations or segmentation results.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 6 questions per image for MSCOCO evaluation
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere all at once) for automatic image segmentation and object extraction
rai:dataSocialImpact: The work addresses object hallucination in LVLMs, which can lead to serious safety issues in real-world applications such as autonomous driving systems making wrong decisions due to incorrect understanding of the external environment. The hallucination phenomenon degrades model performance and harms user experiences in real-world deployment.
rai:dataBiases: The evaluation reveals that LVLMs are prone to hallucinate: (1) frequently appearing objects in the visual instruction datasets (top 10 frequent objects comprise approximately 50-56% of hallucinated objects); (2) objects that frequently co-occur with ground-truth objects in the image (top 10 co-occurring objects comprise 53-71% of hallucinated objects). The object distribution in visual instruction datasets (mostly based on MSCOCO) is unbalanced, with top frequent objects occupying a major part.
rai:dataLimitations: The work only focuses on coarse-grained object hallucinations at the object level, leaving fine-grained hallucinations such as object number, attributes, and positions for future work. Evaluation is conducted on a subset of validation sets due to computational resource limitations. When combined with automatic segmentation tools, objects are annotated based on the tool's label set, which may be inconsistent with human annotations. The matching-based method to determine Yes/No answers may be inaccurate when LVLMs fail to provide explicit answers. The evaluation does not measure overall LVLM performance and higher scores do not necessarily indicate stronger overall capacity.
rai:dataUseCases: POPE is designed for evaluating object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. It can be used to assess the degree of hallucination across different LVLMs and provides a more stable and flexible evaluation method compared to instruction-based approaches like CHAIR. The method can be extended to unannotated datasets using automatic segmentation tools.
